title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Restriction point. Checks a favourable environment and sufficient cell size (N/C ratio); past it, no return. p53 and pRb act here.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: G2/M checkpoint. Checks that all DNA is replicated, in amount and quality.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Metaphase checkpoint. Checks chromosomes are aligned and attached to the spindle; failure triggers apoptosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: G1 phase. Cell growth; non-dividing cells (neurons, lens cells) leave into G0.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: G2 phase. Preparation for division.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: M phase. Prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: S phase. DNA replication; nuclear pores fewer (~2,000).
Interphase G1, S (DNA replication), G2; M phase (prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) + cytokinesis; G0 for non-dividing cells.
G1/S restriction point (environment, size), G2/M (DNA replicated correctly), metaphase (chromosomes aligned and attached).
Cyclin/CDK activate E2F, SPF, MPF; activators CDC25, Polo kinase, CAK; inhibitors p16, p21, p27, Wee1; p53 and pRb tumour suppressors.
Two membranes, 30 nm perinuclear space, outer continuous with RER, inner lined by the lamina (lamins A, B, C); pores.
Premature ageing due to lamin A mutation: defective chromosome attachment to the lamina deforms the nucleus.
Ribosome factory on rDNA loops from chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21, 22; fibrillar centre (rDNA, rRNA), granular periphery (pre-ribosomes).
Condensed inactive X chromosome in females: number = X chromosomes − 1.
Import: NLS, importin α/β, Nup358, FxFG, Nup153, RanGTP dissociation. Export: NES, exportin-1 + RanGTP, RanGAP hydrolysis releases cargo.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Actin microfilaments. G-actin monomers carrying ATP polymerise into two twisted F-actin chains, nucleated by ARP2/3.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Actin roles. Cell cortex, microvilli, vesicle traffic, cytokinesis contractile ring, diapedesis, migration; myosin II contraction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intermediate filaments. Two-headed monomers form dimers, then tetramers, then rope-like filaments; they do not cycle.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: IF roles. Mechanical strength and shape; nuclear lamina (lamins); cytokeratin, desmin, vimentin, neurofilaments, GFAP identify tumour origin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Microtubules. α/β-tubulin dimers (GTP) form protofilaments; 13 protofilaments on γ-TuRC make a tube; stabilised by MAP2.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: MT roles. Mitotic spindle, cilia and flagella, centrioles, axons, organelle transport by kinesin and dynein.
~70% water, small molecules (ions, gases, glucose, amino acids), macromolecules (proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, RNA), inclusions (proteasomes, lipid droplets, glycogen).
Actin microfilaments 5-8 nm, intermediate filaments 8-10 nm, microtubules 20-30 nm.
G-actin (ATP) → F-actin via ARP2/3; cortex, microvilli, vesicle traffic, contractile ring, diapedesis, migration.
ARP2/3, CapZ, tropomyosin, troponin, myosin II (contraction), myosin I (cortex-membrane), severin, fimbrin/filamin/actinin.
α/β-tubulin dimers (GTP) → protofilaments → 13 on γ-TuRC → microtubule; MAP2 stabilises; catastrophe when unbalanced.
Spindle, cilia, flagella, centrioles, axons, transport by kinesin and dynein.
Colchicine, vinblastine, vincristine: block polymerisation. Taxol: blocks depolymerisation.
Cytokeratin (carcinoma), desmin (muscle), vimentin (sarcoma), neurofilaments (neuroblastoma), GFAP (glioma); lamins form the nuclear lamina.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Active transport. Against the gradient using ATP: the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; MDR/ABC pumps expel drugs (chemotherapy, antimalarial resistance).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Endocytosis. Membrane invaginates on clathrin to form a vesicle that fuses with a lysosome; phagocytosis (solids: macrophages, Kupffer cells, osteoclasts) or pinocytosis (liquids).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Exocytosis. Vesicle migrates to the membrane, SNARE proteins fuse the two membranes, and the content is released (saliva, hormones, pancreatic zymogens).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Facilitated diffusion. Down the gradient with a protein: ion channels, aquaporins (water), carriers such as GLUT4 (glucose), which change shape.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Simple diffusion. Down the gradient, no carrier, no ATP: gases, water, some ions, small uncharged molecules (urea).
Asymmetric fluid mosaic; red cell: 40% lipids, 50% proteins, 10% carbohydrates.
Phospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + choline/inositol/serine/ethanolamine. Cholesterol: OH group, 4 rings, hydrocarbon chain; limits permeability.
Peripheral (hydrophilic, e.g. clathrin, G proteins) and integral/transmembrane (pumps, carriers, channels).
Glycolipids and glycoproteins on the extracellular face only; protective, antigenic cell coat.
Simple diffusion (gases, water, small uncharged molecules) and facilitated diffusion (channels, aquaporins, carriers like GLUT4).
Binds Na⁺ inside, phosphorylated by ATP, releases Na⁺ outside, binds K⁺, dephosphorylated, releases K⁺ inside; 1 ATP per cycle (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in).
Endocytosis: clathrin-coated invagination → vesicle → lysosome (phagocytosis, pinocytosis). Exocytosis: vesicle fuses via SNARE and releases content.
GPCR → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA; GPCR → PLC → IP3 (Ca²⁺) + DAG → PKC; RTK → MAP kinase (mitosis); death receptors → apoptosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Confocal microscope. Improved fluorescence microscope with higher resolution and better localisation of the signal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fluorescence microscope. LM with a UV lamp to detect fluorescent labels; helps specify the type of cancer.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Light microscope. Lamp, condenser, objective (4×, 10×, 100×), eyepiece (10×); observes cell structure, confirms diagnosis on biopsies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inverted microscope. Lamp above, objective below the stage; observes living, unstained cells in culture (e.g. embryos in assisted reproduction).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Scanning EM. Electron beam scans the surface, detector and converter give 3D images of cells, bacteria, viruses.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:cellbio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transmission EM. Electron source, magnetic lenses, vacuum pump; sees organelles (e.g. demyelinated axons in prion disease).
Morphological (microscopy), biochemical (electrophoresis, chromatography, ELISA), physiological (cell culture).
Light source, condenser (focuses light), objective (4×, 10×, 100×), eyepiece (10×); base, arm, optical tube.
Fluorescence (UV, labelled cells), confocal (higher-resolution fluorescence), inverted (living unstained cultured cells).
TEM: electron beam, magnetic lenses, vacuum, internal ultrastructure (~100,000×). SEM: scans surface, 3D images of cells, bacteria, viruses.
Drop at slide edge, spread with a second slide, air-dry, stain with MGG.
Sampling, fixation (Bouin), inclusion (paraffin), sectioning (3-4 µm microtome), staining (HE, HES).
HE: haematoxylin nuclei blue, eosin cytoplasm pink. HES: plus saffron, fibres yellow.
37 °C, pH 7-7.4, 5% CO₂ incubator, sterility (hood, UV), sterile vessels, MEM/RPMI 1640 medium with serum and antibiotics.
Tissue sample, mechanical then enzymatic (trypsin) dissociation, count, add medium (~10⁶/10 mL), incubate, daily counts, subculture.
